steps.intro: Mark each statement Holds or Fails. Add a note wherever my wording is off.

steps.headline: The goal is new UI that a fresh agent gets right on the first try, with no rounds of correction.
steps.changed: Today a new screen usually takes several decks of fixes before it looks like YouCoded.
steps.notice: Success is measured by how often a first design comes back with no changes from you.

steps.headline: This work covers the written and visual design guidance only, not the approval process or decks.
steps.changed: The deck and approval process is being redone in a separate session.
steps.notice: Problems I found with decks themselves (about 13% of your pushbacks: no picture, no context) get handed to that session, not fixed here.

steps.headline: The biggest cause of misses is agents inventing their own version of something the app already has.
steps.changed: Six reviewers read about 1,145 of your pushbacks since August. Every one ranked this first: hand-made error boxes, buttons, cards, dropdowns, fades.
steps.notice: The fix usually landed only once you named the existing piece yourself, often after three to six rounds.
steps.resolved: Recorded as a rule for the rebuild: a new piece is allowed when nothing existing fits, but it is built from the app's parts and must look like a sibling of them, never out of place.

steps.headline: Written rules alone do not stick. Approved examples to copy and approved pictures to match would have prevented most misses.
steps.changed: About 60% of pushbacks pointed to a missing example or picture, 18% to a missing rule. Several mistakes kept happening after a rule existed, like buttons at the bottom-left.
steps.notice: The rebuild leads with things to copy and look at, and keeps rules short.

steps.headline: The written guide should be general rules plus pointers to real screens, not a description of every screen.
steps.changed: Your words from an earlier deck: "this should be about more general rules/principles/design instructions that will apply when building new surfaces, with only pointers to existing surfaces to reference."
steps.notice: Today's guide is 935 lines. The rebuilt one is much shorter.
steps.resolved: The rebuilt guide comes back to you on a deck to review before it replaces today's guide.

steps.headline: You want one visual reference you can point at: every building block, every ready-made example, every screen.
steps.changed: Nothing like this exists. Today there is an icon sheet, a status-pill sheet and an old August screenshot gallery.
steps.notice: You could say "I want this popup, with that notice, and those buttons" by pointing at named things.

steps.headline: The kit is drawn by the app's real code, so it can never drift from what the app looks like.
steps.changed: The August screenshot gallery went out of date within weeks because it was pictures, not the real pieces.
steps.notice: Change a button in the app and the kit shows the new button automatically.

steps.headline: Outdated and contradictory design docs get archived or fixed as part of this work.
steps.changed: Several docs disagree with each other or still describe rules you reversed, such as a filled "Back to chat" button.
steps.notice: One current source for each rule. Old records stay in the archive as history.

steps.intro: Scope questions, answered in words. How the kit looks comes later, as drawn designs.

steps.headline: The kit is a YouCoded Page that updates itself. Should it be a new tab on the Work board, or its own page?
steps.today: The Work board is a YouCoded Page that redraws from the newest code each time you open it, and already has a Screens tab. Its screen pictures are from Oct 12 to 16 and have not refreshed since.
steps.checked: Read the Work board's page files and its Screens tab code 2026-11-18; the pictures were last committed 2026-10-16.
steps.problem: A Page cannot run the app's live pieces, so it shows pictures of them. Pictures go stale unless something retakes them, as the Screens tab shows.
steps.proposal: Either way: the page redraws from the newest code when opened, and its pictures, the kit's and the Screens tab's, are retaken automatically whenever a change to the app's look lands. Agents still copy the real code.

options.label: A tab on the Work board
options.summary: A Design kit tab beside Screens. Each piece and example links straight to the screens that use it, in the same page.
pros: One page for screens and pieces; "where is this used" is one click.
Uses the page you already open every day.
cons: The Work board gets one more tab.
Only on your devices, like the Work board; not something other users get.

options.label: Its own page
options.summary: A separate Design kit page in your Pages, linking out to the Work board's Screens tab.
pros: Focused: nothing but design.
cons: "Where is this used" jumps between two pages.

steps.headline: The Work board already shows every screen. Should the kit build on its Screens tab instead of a second gallery?
steps.today: The Work board's Screens tab shows every photographed screen, grouped by kind, with search, filters and click paths. It does not say which pieces each screen uses.
steps.checked: Read the Screens tab code 2026-11-18: it groups by screen kind and place, with no link to shared pieces.
steps.problem: A second screen gallery would duplicate it. But to see where a button or error box is used, screens need to know their pieces.
steps.proposal: Pieces and examples are built first, together. Then screens and pieces get linked both ways.

options.label: Extend the Screens tab
options.summary: Each screen gains its list of pieces and examples, worked out automatically when it is photographed; each piece links back. Its pictures start refreshing automatically too.
pros: No duplicate gallery.
Answers "where is this used" from either side.
cons: Touches the Work board's existing tab, so it comes back to you on a deck.

options.label: Leave screens out
options.summary: The kit shows pieces and examples only; each lists screen names, not pictures.
pros: Smaller; the Work board is untouched.
cons: No pictures of where a piece is used, and the Screens tab stays stale.

steps.headline: The first ready-made examples, picked from the mistakes you corrected most often

calls.why: A small popup that does one thing, one card holding its words, box and stacked buttons. Took six decks to settle.

more.today: Each new small popup was laid out differently.
more.problem: Grey hint placement and button position were corrected again and again.
more.change: One approved example every new small popup copies.

calls.why: The one tinted box, its sentence, a Details fold, buttons inside at the right. Hand-made versions were corrected about 20 times.

more.today: Agents kept drawing their own warning and error boxes.
more.problem: You had to say "use the existing style" in many decks.
more.change: Info, warning, error and unknown-error versions to copy.

calls.why: When Send, Install or Download fails: the notice takes the buttons' place and keeps what you wrote.

more.today: Failures were drawn differently on each screen.
more.problem: Retry above the details, two light buttons, no main button.
more.change: One example of a failure replacing its buttons.

calls.why: One, two and three buttons: side by side, stacked, red confirm, costs money. Bottom-left buttons were corrected in about ten decks.

more.today: Button placement is described in words only.
more.problem: Filled buttons kept landing at the bottom-left or unbalanced.
more.change: Every approved arrangement shown, wide and narrow.

calls.why: A small label over one card of rows with switches, a fold-out row and a full-width follow-up button.

more.today: Settings screens were rebuilt by hand each time.
more.problem: Bare text on the popup, boxes in boxes, folds opening a separate card.

calls.why: Labelled cards, the body scrolling under a fade, buttons pinned to the bottom line.

more.today: Close session and Submit a ticket do this, but nothing points to them as the pattern.
more.problem: Buttons ended up under the last card or inside it.
more.change: One example with the pinned bottom line.

calls.why: Something you open from a card: top card with name, status, chips and actions, then two columns.

more.today: Only the Marketplace detail pages follow it.
more.problem: New detail views kept inventing their own layout.
more.change: One example any new detail view copies.

calls.why: Raised cards for things you open or install: name and status, one chip row that scrolls sideways, two lines of description.

more.problem: Chips of different sizes, wrapping chip rows, flat cards.

calls.why: The small menu under a control, a dropdown, a quick picker with search, and a list's manage row at the foot.

more.problem: Menus with their own shape, transparent menus, missing fades.
more.change: One example of each list kind.

calls.why: First-time card with one button, the quiet nothing-picked line, the loading line, and a whole screen that cannot load.

more.today: These exist as pieces but not shown in place.
more.problem: Empty screens with a small notice at the top, dead-end error states.
more.change: Each state shown in a real screen frame.

calls.call: Chips, pills and tags in a row
calls.why: Status pills with dots, fact chips, tags and filter chips beside a search box, all the same height.

more.problem: Mismatched heights and roundness, text sitting too high beside a dot, corrected over several decks.
more.change: One example lining them up together.

calls.why: Which surface a new feature uses: top-bar button opens a panel or full screen, popups only from Settings or a status chip.

more.problem: Wrong surface was one of the most common arrangement misses.
more.change: One example of each, with where each opens from.

steps.headline: What should happen to today's written design guide?
steps.today: The guide is 935 lines: nine principles, recipes for every kind of element, sections describing seven unreviewed screens, and 22 open questions.
steps.problem: Agents read it and still guess what the words look like. The screen-by-screen descriptions are what you said the guide should not be.
steps.proposal: Pick what the written guide becomes once the kit exists.

options.label: Short guide that points at the kit
options.summary: Principles, a 'which example do I use' table, a short wording guide, and pointers into the kit. Screen descriptions move to their own notes.
pros: Quick to read; every rule has a picture beside it in the kit.
One place for each rule.
cons: Rewording 935 lines takes care not to lose a decision.

options.label: Keep it, add kit links
options.summary: Leave the guide as is and link each recipe to its kit example.
pros: Nothing you approved is reworded.
cons: Stays long; agents still read prose first.

options.label: Kit replaces it
options.summary: Rules live only as captions in the kit; no separate written guide.
pros: Nothing to keep in sync.
cons: Rules that are not about one piece have nowhere obvious to live.

steps.headline: When should the guide's 22 open questions be answered?
steps.today: The guide lists 22 questions you have not ruled on, such as where buttons sit beside text and how multi-step popups show their steps.
steps.checked: Counted in the guide 2026-11-18; numbered Q1 to Q23 with no Q10.
steps.problem: These are exactly where agents guess. About 18% of pushbacks were a case no rule covered.

options.label: As each example needs them
options.summary: Each question is asked with pictures when the example it affects is designed.
pros: You decide with pictures, not words.
No long question deck up front.
cons: Questions no example touches stay open longer.

options.label: All now
options.summary: One or two decks answer all 22 before the kit is built.
pros: Everything settled early.
cons: Many would be words-only, which you said is hard to judge.

steps.headline: Should automatic checks catch the mistakes you corrected most often?
steps.today: Some checks exist: hand-made popups, notice boxes and toggles fail the build. Button placement, lines across boxes and chip heights are not checked.
steps.checked: Checked the app's check rules and tests 2026-11-18.
steps.problem: Buttons at the bottom-left and hand-styled buttons kept coming back even after you ruled on them.
steps.proposal: Add checks for the repeat mistakes that can be measured. You would never see them, only fewer misses.

options.label: Add them
options.summary: Checks for filled buttons at the bottom-left, lines across boxes, hand-styled buttons and mismatched heights in a row.
pros: A repeat mistake is stopped before you ever see it.
cons: Some extra build time; a check may need tuning if it flags a fine design.

options.label: Not now
options.summary: Rely on the kit and the guide.
pros: Less to build.
cons: Repeat mistakes still reach you sometimes.

steps.headline: Should the guide include a short wording guide?
steps.today: Wording rules are scattered: sentence case, Try again, plain words. Too-long or jargon copy was about 14% of pushbacks.
steps.problem: Agents kept adding grey helper text, duplicate headings and words like "bookkeeping" or "join".
steps.proposal: A one-page wording guide: good and bad examples, a word budget per kind of text, and a list of words to avoid.

options.label: Include it
options.summary: Short, with real before and after examples from your decks.
pros: Fewer rounds on copy.
cons: Wording is still edited on real screens last; this only makes the first try better.

options.label: Leave wording out
options.summary: Keep wording to the final pass on real screens.
pros: Smaller rebuild.
cons: Copy keeps coming back long.

steps.headline: Should the kit for Pages (apps people build in YouCoded) share the same examples?
steps.today: Pages have their own style kit that copies some app pieces by hand. You asked on Oct 8 for it to be "directly tied to the real app ui".
steps.checked: Card 90 and the decisions log, read 2026-11-18.
steps.problem: Two separate kits drift apart, and Pages guidance falls behind the app.
steps.proposal: Decide whether Pages join this rebuild now or later.

options.label: Later, on its own
options.summary: Build the app kit first; Pages adopt its examples in a follow-up.
pros: This work stays focused.
Pages get examples that are already approved.
cons: Pages guidance stays behind a little longer.

options.label: Include now
options.summary: Every example also comes in a Pages version.
pros: One kit for both from the start.
cons: Roughly doubles the example work.

steps.resolved: Noted on card 90 (Pages): once this kit exists, the Pages kit is rebuilt from its approved examples and reusable pieces.

steps.headline: Should brand mismatches in the app be fixed in this work?
steps.today: The app's YouCoded themes still use the old purple, and setup still says "agents for everyone", a line the brand guide retired.
steps.checked: The brand guide lists both as known gaps, read 2026-11-18.
steps.problem: They are visible to users, so they need your approval either way.
steps.proposal: Decide whether they ride along here or get their own small piece of work.

options.label: Separate small change
options.summary: Filed as its own card, shown to you on its own deck.
pros: Users see the change; it deserves its own look.
cons: One more small thing on the list.

options.label: Include here
options.summary: Fixed alongside the guide clean-up.
pros: Done sooner.
cons: Mixes a visible app change into docs work.

steps.headline: Anything about how you picture the kit? Skip if nothing comes to mind.
steps.today: Nothing is drawn yet. The next stage shows two to four drawn designs of the kit page.
steps.checked: No kit designs exist as of 2026-11-18.
steps.problem: Drawings that miss what you already have in mind cost a round.
steps.proposal: A line on what you imagine: a layout, an app it should feel like, what you would do on it first.

steps.page: How the Design kit tab looks
steps.intro: Pick a drawing for each. Drag a box on any picture to comment on that spot.

steps.headline: Three words, everywhere: components, surface templates and surfaces.
steps.changed: Components are the small parts (a button, a switch). A surface template is a design assembled from components. A surface is a real screen, popup or menu in the app, each one a template in action.
steps.notice: The Work board's Screens tab becomes Surfaces, and the rewritten guide uses only these three words.

steps.headline: Which layout shows, at a glance, how components, surface templates and surfaces fit together?
steps.today: The earlier drawings split "examples" and "pieces" into separate groups, so nothing showed how one is built from the other.
steps.checked: From your comments on the earlier drawings, 2026-11-24.
steps.problem: You should understand the page from one look or one click-through: which template is made of which components, and which real surfaces use it. No explainer text.
steps.proposal: Drawn inside the real Work board with its own styles. Pictures inside are a month old and counts are made up.

options.label: A row per template
options.summary: Each template is one row: its picture, then its name and the components it is made of, then the real surfaces using it. Components sit below.
pros: Reads left to right: the template, what it's made of, where it's used.
Every template's links visible without clicking.
cons: About four templates per screen; more scrolling.

from: Work board cards and fact chips

options.label: Three linked columns
options.summary: Components, templates and surfaces side by side. Click a template: its components and its surfaces light up, everything else fades.
pros: The relationship is the layout itself.
Works backwards too: click any of the components to see every template using it.
cons: Needs a click before the connections show.
Small pictures in the middle column.

from: Filter pills as the list of components

options.label: Stacked tiles
options.summary: Each template is a tile with its real surfaces fanned behind it and its components along its foot. Components have their own tab.
pros: Most pictures per screen.
The stack shows "one design, many uses" at a glance.
cons: Surfaces behind are only hinted at until you click.
Components are a tab away.

steps.reopened: You liked none of the first three layouts and found "examples" and "pieces" unclear.
steps.reframed: Renamed to components, surface templates and surfaces, and redrew every layout so its structure shows how they connect.

steps.path: Design kit tab → a piece or example
steps.headline: What should open when you click an example or piece?
steps.today: Clicking a screen on the Screens tab opens a popup: its picture on the left, where it is and its facts on the right, two buttons at the foot.
steps.checked: Opened a screen's popup on the Work board 2026-11-18.
steps.problem: An example has several versions (error, warning, unknown error), rules, a don't, and dozens of screens that use it. It has to fit without becoming a wall of text.
steps.proposal: Drawn inside the real Work board with its own styles. The screen pictures inside are a month old and the counts are made up; the real tab has live ones.

options.label: Same popup as Screens
options.summary: Picture on the left with a pill row to switch versions; its job, rules, a don't and the screens using it on the right.
pros: Matches the Screens popup exactly, arrows to step through included.
Short: one version's picture at a time.
cons: You switch versions one at a time instead of seeing them side by side.

from: Screens popup: header, arrows, picture, facts column, footer buttons
Filter pills as the version switch
new: Rules, Don't and Used on sections

options.label: Every version at once
options.summary: One column: a line on its job, every version side by side, a Do and Don't pair, then a strip of screens that use it.
pros: All versions compared at a glance.
Do and Don't shown as a pair.
cons: Taller; scrolls on a laptop.
Looks different from the Screens popup.

steps.headline: What should a surface's popup add, now that it belongs to a template?
steps.today: A surface's popup on the Surfaces tab shows its picture, where it is, its kind and how many clicks reach it.
steps.checked: Opened the Close session surface's popup on the Work board 2026-11-24.
steps.problem: The earlier drawing listed all its components and read as busy and repetitive. The template already lists its components.
steps.proposal: Add only what is new: which template it follows. Drawn inside the real Work board with its own styles. Pictures inside are a month old and counts are made up.

options.label: Its template, one button
options.summary: One line: the template it follows, as a button that opens it in the Design kit.
pros: Quietest: one line added.
Components are one click away, on the template.
cons: You don't see from here when a surface strayed from its template.

options.label: Plus a hand-made flag
options.summary: The same line, plus a small tag only when the surface has a part not built from the components.
pros: Surfaces that drifted from the kit stand out.
cons: One more tag on some popups.

steps.reopened: You found the earlier list too busy and repetitive.
